figures.alt: A Florentine Codex drawing of Nahua smallpox victims lying on woven mats, covered in spots, with one person leaning over a sick patient.
figures.caption: Nahua victims of smallpox, Florentine Codex, Book 12, c. 1585.

books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

primary_sources: Florentine Codex, Book 12, c. 1585, public domain

options.text: Smallpox was brought to the Americas deliberately, as a Spanish weapon of war.
options.misconception: The image shows victims of an epidemic, not a deliberate attack; the disease spread through contact, and no source shows the Spanish spreading it on purpose in this period.

options.text: The disease struck whole households at once, leaving the sick unable to move.
Smallpox arrived in the Americas from Africa with enslaved laborers.
options.misconception: Smallpox came from Europe with the colonists; the large-scale African slave trade grew later and did not bring the first epidemics.

options.text: Native peoples had immunity to smallpox from earlier exposure to the disease.
options.misconception: The victims are covered in sores and lying helpless; the image shows a people with no immunity at all.

rationales.A: Nothing in the image shows a deliberate attack. The disease spread through contact after 1492; using it as a weapon came much later, if at all.
rationales.B: The drawing shows people lying on mats, covered in spots, too sick to rise, with bodies lying still beside them. Smallpox hit whole households at the same time, so there was no one left healthy enough to tend the sick or bury the dead.
rationales.C: The direction is wrong. Smallpox sailed west from Europe with the first colonists, before the large-scale African slave trade began.
rationales.D: The image proves the opposite. The victims are covered in sores and cannot move; a people with immunity would not fall sick in such numbers.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the house in the drawing. Sick people lie on mats, covered in spots, too ill to sit up.
2. Ask who is missing. Nobody stands to nurse the sick or bury the dead, because whole households fell ill together.
3. Ask where the sickness came from. Smallpox crossed from Europe, where people had lived with it for centuries; in the Americas no one had immunity.
4. Rule out the rest. The image shows an epidemic, not a weapon, and the disease came from Europe, not Africa.
Remember: when a disease strikes everyone at once, look for a people with no immunity, not for a stronger weapon.

stem: This drawing from the Florentine Codex shows Nahua people suffering from smallpox in central Mexico in the 1500s. What does the image show about the epidemic?

stimulus.source_note: Florentine Codex, Book 12, c. 1585, public domain, Wikimedia Commons. Image viewed before writing.
stimulus.text: This drawing from the Florentine Codex, Book 12, shows Nahua people suffering from smallpox in central Mexico in the 1500s. On the left, a sick person covered in spots lies on a mat while another person leans over them. On the right, bodies covered in spots lie still on woven mats, unable to move.
